subject: biology
topicDisplay: C1 — Interaction and interdependence: enzymes, respiration and photosynthesis
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Enzymes speed up reactions without being used up
Anabolism builds and uses energy; catabolism breaks down and releases it
Enzyme and substrate both change shape as they bind
Temperature, pH and substrate concentration change the rate
Pathways run as a line or as a cycle
ATP carries energy from where it is released to where it is used
Respiration makes ATP inside cells; gas exchange is something else
Making lactate keeps glycolysis running without oxygen
Yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide instead
The Krebs cycle oxidizes acetyl groups and regenerates oxaloacetate
Protons flow back through ATP synthase, making ATP
Lipids give more energy per gram but need oxygen
Light energy becomes chemical energy in carbon compounds
Oxygen is left over from splitting water
Pigments absorb only certain wavelengths, exciting electrons
Absorption spectra and action spectra look alike but measure different things
Growing plants in extra carbon dioxide to predict the future
Photosystem II splits water and releases oxygen
Photosystem I reduces NADP
Each set of reactions depends on the other

questions.q: Catalase in liver cells increases the rate at which hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen by a factor of many millions. What is the benefit to the cell of this increase in rate?
options: Hydrogen peroxide could not be broken down at all without an enzyme to make it possible.
Toxic hydrogen peroxide is removed fast enough at cell temperature to prevent damage.
Catalase supplies the energy that the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide needs.
The reaction releases energy that the cell captures as ATP, as in respiration.
optionWhy: A student who thinks enzymes make reactions possible rather than faster picks this. In fact hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly on its own; catalase increases the rate enormously.

The benefit of increasing rates of reaction in cells is that reactions which would be uselessly slow at cell temperature happen fast enough to be useful. Here a toxic substance is destroyed before it can harm the cell.
A student who thinks enzymes provide energy picks this. In fact catalase lowers the activation energy; it does not supply energy to the substrate.

A student who thinks every metabolic reaction is an energy-yielding reaction like respiration picks this. In fact the cell does not harvest energy from this reaction; its purpose is to remove a toxic product.
questions.explain: The benefit of increasing rates of reaction in cells is that reactions which would be uselessly slow at cell temperature happen fast enough to be useful. Here a toxic substance is destroyed before it can harm the cell.

questions.q: In the small intestine, maltase converts each maltose molecule into two glucose molecules. How is this reaction classified?
options: Anabolic; the glucose produced is a useful new molecule that the body can then absorb and make use of
Catabolic; a hydrolysis reaction in which a water molecule is used to break the glycosidic bond
Catabolic; a condensation reaction in which a water molecule is released as the bond is broken
Catabolic; energy from ATP is needed to force the two glucose units of the maltose apart
optionWhy: A student who judges by whether the product is useful picks this. In fact the classification depends on the substrate being broken into smaller molecules, which makes it catabolic.
Digestion of a larger molecule into monomers is catabolism, and the bond between the two glucose units is broken by the addition of water, which is hydrolysis.
A student who attaches water release to bond breaking picks this. In fact condensation joins monomers and releases water; breaking the bond uses water and is hydrolysis.
A student who thinks breaking molecules down needs an input of energy picks this. In fact hydrolysis in digestion releases energy overall and does not consume ATP.
questions.explain: Digestion of a larger molecule into monomers is catabolism, and the bond between the two glucose units is broken by the addition of water, which is hydrolysis.

questions.q: According to the induced-fit model, what happens when a substrate binds to the active site of an enzyme?
options: The rigid active site admits only an exactly matching substrate.
The active site closes around a substrate that keeps its shape.
The enzyme seizes the substrate and holds it without any changes.
Both the enzyme and the substrate change shape as they bind.
optionWhy: A student still using the lock-and-key model picks this. In fact the active site is not rigid: it changes shape as the substrate binds.
A student who has noticed only the enzyme's movement picks this. In fact the substrate also changes shape on binding, and that change weakens its bonds.
A student who imagines enzymes actively catching substrates picks this. In fact substrate and active site meet by random collision, and both change shape once bound.
Students should recognize that both substrate and enzyme change shape when binding occurs. The closer fit strains bonds within the substrate, which is part of how catalysis is achieved.
questions.explain: Students should recognize that both substrate and enzyme change shape when binding occurs. The closer fit strains bonds within the substrate, which is part of how catalysis is achieved.

questions.q: A textbook sketch graph shows the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction rising steadily with temperature to a sharp peak and then falling steeply. A class measured catalase activity every 5 °C from 5 °C to 70 °C and found a broad plateau between 30 °C and 45 °C rather than a sharp peak. How should the sketch graph be regarded?
options: As an accurate record of catalase results, which shows that the class must have made an error somewhere.
As a model that the mismatch has proved to be wrong, so it should be discarded and not used again.
As a model of the general relationship, which the class data can be used to evaluate and refine.
As a graph of one specific enzyme that was measured, so it says nothing about catalase.
optionWhy: A student who treats a sketch graph as data picks this. In fact a sketch has no data points or scale; it is a simplified model and cannot overrule real measurements.
A student who thinks a model is simply right or wrong picks this. In fact a mismatch leads to evaluation and refinement; the general pattern of rise, optimum and fall is still supported.

Generalized sketches of relationships are models. The class results neither prove nor disprove the sketch outright; they are evidence for evaluating it, and here suggest that for catalase the peak should be drawn as a plateau.
A student who thinks the sketch records one enzyme's results picks this. In fact it is a generalized model intended to apply to enzymes in general, which is exactly why catalase data can test it.
questions.explain: Generalized sketches of relationships are models. The class results neither prove nor disprove the sketch outright; they are evidence for evaluating it, and here suggest that for catalase the peak should be drawn as a plateau.

questions.q: What distinguishes the Calvin cycle and the Krebs cycle from glycolysis?
options: The cycles regenerate all of their intermediates and so produce no net product, whereas glycolysis produces pyruvate as its end product.
In the cycles an intermediate used in the first step is regenerated in the last, whereas glycolysis runs from glucose to pyruvate in a chain.
The cycles use up their starting compound on every turn, so it must be supplied continuously from outside, unlike the glucose used in glycolysis.
The cycles take place in the gut, where food is broken down to release its energy, whereas glycolysis takes place inside cells.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a cycle makes nothing new picks this. In fact substrates enter and products leave each cycle: the Krebs cycle releases carbon dioxide and reduced NAD, and the Calvin cycle releases triose phosphate.

A cyclical pathway regenerates one intermediate with each turn: RuBP in the Calvin cycle and oxaloacetate in the Krebs cycle. Glycolysis is linear, converting glucose through a series of intermediates to pyruvate with nothing regenerated.
A student who applies linear-pathway logic to cycles picks this. In fact the starting compound of a cycle is what is regenerated; it is glycolysis whose starting substrate, glucose, is consumed.
A student who conflates the Krebs cycle with digestion picks this. In fact both cycles are intracellular: the Krebs cycle in mitochondria and the Calvin cycle in chloroplasts.
questions.explain: A cyclical pathway regenerates one intermediate with each turn: RuBP in the Calvin cycle and oxaloacetate in the Krebs cycle. Glycolysis is linear, converting glucose through a series of intermediates to pyruvate with nothing regenerated.

questions.q: A cell needs an energy currency that can supply many different reactions in the cytoplasm. Which property makes ATP suitable for this role?
options: It holds a very large amount of energy, so that a cell can store it for many weeks between meals.
It releases energy in an amount suited to a single reaction and is quickly re-formed from ADP.
It is consumed after one use, so the cell then builds fresh ATP directly from glucose.
It acts as an enzyme, catalysing each of the reactions in the cytoplasm that need energy.
optionWhy: A student who thinks ATP is a long-term store picks this. In fact ATP is used within seconds of being formed; energy for weeks is stored as glycogen and lipid, not as ATP.
ATP hydrolysis releases a modest packet of energy, enough for many individual tasks, and ADP is phosphorylated back to ATP within seconds, so a small pool of ATP can supply energy continuously.
A student who thinks ATP is used up and replaced from scratch picks this. In fact ATP is recycled: the ADP and phosphate formed by hydrolysis are rejoined using energy from respiration.
A student who thinks ATP is a protein or enzyme picks this. In fact ATP is a nucleotide; it supplies energy by being hydrolysed, and the reactions are catalysed by separate enzymes.
questions.explain: ATP hydrolysis releases a modest packet of energy, enough for many individual tasks, and ADP is phosphorylated back to ATP within seconds, so a small pool of ATP can supply energy continuously.

questions.q: A student writes: 'Cell respiration is when oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it in the lungs.' Which statement correctly evaluates this?
options: It is wrong: this describes gas exchange; cell respiration releases energy from carbon compounds to make ATP inside cells.
It is right: respiration is the exchange of gases at a respiratory surface, which the cells then make use of.
It is wrong: cell respiration is glucose reacting with oxygen inside cells, and glucose is the only substrate used.
It is wrong: cell respiration creates the energy a cell needs, using the oxygen that gas exchange brings into the body.
optionWhy: Gas exchange is the movement of gases across a surface. Cell respiration is a chemical process in every cell that releases energy from carbon compounds to produce ATP; the two must be distinguished.

A student who uses the everyday meaning of 'respiration' as breathing picks this. In fact gas exchange supplies oxygen to and removes carbon dioxide from cells; respiration is what happens inside them.

A student who defines respiration by the glucose equation picks this. In fact glucose and fatty acids are the principal substrates, but a wide range of carbon compounds can be respired; the statement is wrong because it describes gas exchange, not because it omits glucose.

A student who thinks respiration creates energy picks this. In fact energy cannot be created; respiration releases energy already held in carbon compounds and transfers it to ATP, and the statement is wrong because it describes gas exchange.
questions.explain: Gas exchange is the movement of gases across a surface. Cell respiration is a chemical process in every cell that releases energy from carbon compounds to produce ATP; the two must be distinguished.

questions.q: During intense exercise, muscle cells convert pyruvate to lactate. What is the purpose of this conversion?
options: To release extra ATP from pyruvate once the mitochondria have stopped working.
To oxidize pyruvate so that more reduced NAD is available to the cell.
To regenerate NAD so that glycolysis can continue producing ATP.
To convert pyruvate into a form able to enter the mitochondria.
optionWhy: A student who thinks lactate formation is where the anaerobic ATP comes from picks this. In fact no ATP is formed in this step; all the ATP comes from glycolysis.
A student who assumes every step of respiration is an oxidation picks this. In fact pyruvate is reduced, accepting hydrogen from reduced NAD, which is thereby oxidized back to NAD.
Reducing pyruvate to lactate converts reduced NAD back to NAD. This allows glycolysis, which needs NAD for its oxidation step, to continue with a net yield of two ATP per glucose.
A student who thinks all respiration passes through mitochondria picks this. In fact lactate formation occurs when oxygen is insufficient and the mitochondrial pathway cannot be used.
questions.explain: Reducing pyruvate to lactate converts reduced NAD back to NAD. This allows glycolysis, which needs NAD for its oxidation step, to continue with a net yield of two ATP per glucose.

questions.q: Yeast is used in baking to make dough rise and in brewing to make beer alcoholic. Which statement explains both uses?
options: Anaerobic respiration of sugars produces carbon dioxide, which raises the dough, and ethanol, which remains in the beer.
The carbon dioxide that raises dough comes from aerobic respiration, since anaerobic respiration releases none.
Yeast produces lactate, as human muscle does, which sours the dough and makes the beer alcoholic.
Yeast uses the small amount of oxygen dissolved in the dough or beer to produce carbon dioxide and ethanol.
optionWhy: In anaerobic respiration yeast converts glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide. Bubbles of carbon dioxide make dough rise (the ethanol evaporates in baking), while the ethanol is the alcohol in beer.
A student who generalises from human anaerobic respiration picks this. In fact yeast releases carbon dioxide anaerobically, by decarboxylating pyruvate, which is what makes dough rise.
A student who thinks all anaerobic respiration gives lactate picks this. In fact yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; lactate is not alcoholic and is not a yeast product.
A student who thinks anaerobic respiration uses a little oxygen picks this. In fact ethanol is produced only when oxygen is absent; the pathway needs no oxygen at all.
questions.explain: In anaerobic respiration yeast converts glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide. Bubbles of carbon dioxide make dough rise (the ethanol evaporates in baking), while the ethanol is the alcohol in beer.

questions.q: One acetyl group enters the Krebs cycle and oxaloacetate is regenerated. Which account of one turn of the cycle is correct?
options: Two carbon dioxide molecules form when oxygen oxidizes the carbon atoms of the acetyl group directly.
Each of the four oxidations forms one ATP directly, so the cycle yields most of the cell's ATP supply.
Only decarboxylation occurs, since no oxygen enters the matrix to oxidize any of the cycle's intermediates.
Two decarboxylations give off carbon dioxide, four dehydrogenations reduce carriers, one ATP forms.
optionWhy: A student who thinks oxygen reacts in the cycle picks this. In fact the oxidations are dehydrogenations and the carbon dioxide comes from decarboxylation, without any oxygen.
A student who attributes most ATP to the cycle picks this. In fact the oxidations reduce NAD; only one ATP per turn is formed directly, and most ATP comes from chemiosmosis.
A student who thinks oxidation needs oxygen picks this. In fact four oxidations occur in each turn by removal of hydrogen, which reduces NAD, with no oxygen involved.
Per turn, two carbons leave as carbon dioxide by decarboxylation, four oxidations by removal of hydrogen produce reduced carriers (mainly reduced NAD), and one ATP is formed directly.
questions.explain: Per turn, two carbons leave as carbon dioxide by decarboxylation, four oxidations by removal of hydrogen produce reduced carriers (mainly reduced NAD), and one ATP is formed directly.

questions.q: A chemical makes the inner mitochondrial membrane freely permeable to protons. Electron flow and oxygen consumption continue, but ATP synthesis stops. Which statement explains these observations?
options: Protons leak back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase, so no gradient remains to drive ADP phosphorylation.
Electrons leak through the membrane instead of reaching oxygen, so no energy arrives at ATP synthase.
Water enters the matrix by osmosis, diluting the ADP and phosphate so that they can no longer be joined together.
Reduced NAD cannot transfer energy directly to ADP, because the leak removes the protons that it needs.
optionWhy: Chemiosmosis needs a proton gradient and a single route back through ATP synthase. If protons can cross the membrane anywhere, the chain still pumps them (so electron flow and oxygen use continue) but no gradient builds up and ATP synthase has nothing to drive it.

A student who thinks electrons cross the membrane picks this, but it contradicts the data: oxygen is still consumed, so electrons are still reaching it. Electrons stay in the carriers; it is protons that leak.
A student who reads chemiosmosis as osmosis picks this. In fact water plays no part; ATP synthesis fails because the proton gradient has been dissipated.
A student who thinks reduced NAD phosphorylates ADP directly picks this. In fact reduced NAD gives electrons to the chain, and the electron flow is unaffected; only the gradient is lost.
questions.explain: Chemiosmosis needs a proton gradient and a single route back through ATP synthase. If protons can cross the membrane anywhere, the chain still pumps them (so electron flow and oxygen use continue) but no gradient builds up and ATP synthase has nothing to drive it.

questions.q: A sprinter's leg muscles rely on anaerobic respiration during a 100 m race. Which statement explains why the muscles cannot use fatty acids to supply this energy?
options: Fatty acids enter aerobic respiration as acetyl-CoA and cannot enter glycolysis, the only stage that yields ATP without oxygen.
Fatty acids must first be converted into glucose, and this conversion is far too slow to keep pace with a sprint.
Fatty acids can be respired anaerobically, but the muscle prefers glucose because it is much faster to break down.
Fatty acids contain too little energy per gram to supply the very large amount of ATP that a sprint needs.
optionWhy: Glycolysis and anaerobic respiration occur only if carbohydrate is the substrate. Fatty acids are converted to acetyl-CoA and oxidized in the Krebs cycle, which depends on the electron transport chain and therefore on oxygen.

A student who thinks all substrates are turned into glucose picks this. In fact fatty acids are not converted to glucose in muscle; they enter respiration as acetyl-CoA, which requires the aerobic pathway.

A student who thinks any substrate can be used without oxygen picks this. In fact fatty acids cannot be respired anaerobically at all, because they bypass glycolysis and enter only the aerobic pathway.

A student who thinks carbohydrate is the richer fuel picks this. In fact lipids hold roughly twice the energy per gram; the problem is that releasing it requires oxygen, which the sprinting muscle lacks.
questions.explain: Glycolysis and anaerobic respiration occur only if carbohydrate is the substrate. Fatty acids are converted to acetyl-CoA and oxidized in the Krebs cycle, which depends on the electron transport chain and therefore on oxygen.

questions.q: A fox eats a rabbit that has fed on grass. Where did the chemical energy in the carbon compounds of the fox's body originally come from?
options: New energy created by the grass in photosynthesis and passed on to the rabbit and fox.
Light energy transformed into chemical energy by photosynthesis in the grass.
Chemical energy that the grass absorbed from the soil through its roots.
Energy in the oxygen the grass made as its main product, breathed in by the two animals.
optionWhy: A student who thinks plants generate energy picks this. Photosynthesis creates no energy; it transforms light energy that already exists into chemical energy in carbon compounds, which passed along the food chain.

The energy transformation in photosynthesis supplies most of the chemical energy needed for life processes in ecosystems: the grass transformed light energy into chemical energy in carbon compounds, which passed to the rabbit and then to the fox.
A student who thinks plants take in food from the soil picks this. In fact the soil supplies water and mineral ions only; the chemical energy of the grass came from light.
A student who sees oxygen as the energy-rich main product of photosynthesis picks this. Oxygen is a by-product; the chemical energy is stored in the carbon compounds, not in the oxygen.
questions.explain: The energy transformation in photosynthesis supplies most of the chemical energy needed for life processes in ecosystems: the grass transformed light energy into chemical energy in carbon compounds, which passed to the rabbit and then to the fox.

questions.q: Algae were supplied with water containing the heavy isotope oxygen-18 and ordinary carbon dioxide; the oxygen gas they released contained oxygen-18. Other algae were given ordinary water and carbon dioxide containing oxygen-18; the oxygen gas they released contained no oxygen-18. What do these results show?
options: The oxygen released by photosynthesis comes from the splitting of water and not from carbon dioxide.
The oxygen released comes from carbon dioxide once its carbon has been removed to make glucose.
Water is not a reactant but only dissolves the carbon dioxide before the reaction takes place.
Producing oxygen is the main purpose of photosynthesis, using both water and carbon dioxide.
optionWhy: The label appears in the oxygen gas only when it is supplied in the water, so the oxygen produced by photosynthesis comes from the splitting of water. The oxygen atoms of carbon dioxide end up in glucose and water.

A student who pictures the plant swapping carbon dioxide for oxygen picks this. The data contradict it: labelled carbon dioxide gave unlabelled oxygen, so none of the released oxygen came from carbon dioxide.
A student who thinks of water as a mere solvent picks this. The appearance of oxygen-18 from labelled water in the oxygen gas shows that water molecules are broken apart during photosynthesis.

A student who sees oxygen as the product the plant is aiming for picks this. The experiment says nothing about purpose, and oxygen is a by-product formed only from water; the useful products are the carbon compounds.
questions.explain: The label appears in the oxygen gas only when it is supplied in the water, so the oxygen produced by photosynthesis comes from the splitting of water. The oxygen atoms of carbon dioxide end up in glucose and water.

questions.q: The absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a has peaks at about 430 nm (blue) and 660 nm (red) but a trough at about 550 nm (green). Which statement best explains this pattern?
options: Green photons carry too little energy to excite an electron in chlorophyll a, whereas blue and red photons both carry more than enough energy to do so.
Only photons whose energy matches that needed to excite an electron in chlorophyll a are absorbed; blue and red photons match, green do not.
Chlorophyll a absorbs green light more strongly than any other colour, which is exactly why leaves that contain it appear green.
Blue and red light heat the chlorophyll molecule more than green light does, so more of their energy is taken in and stored.
optionWhy: A student who treats absorption as a threshold picks this. Green photons (550 nm) carry more energy than red photons (660 nm), yet red is absorbed and green is not, so absorption depends on matching an energy gap, not on exceeding a minimum.

Electron energy levels are discrete, so a photon is absorbed only if its energy matches the gap between the ground state and an available excited state. Blue and red photons match transitions in chlorophyll a; green photons do not, and are reflected or transmitted.

A student who links the colour seen with the colour absorbed picks this. The trough in the spectrum shows green is absorbed least; leaves look green because green light is reflected and transmitted rather than absorbed.

A student who thinks absorbed light acts by heating picks this. Absorption raises an electron to a higher energy level; the pattern of wavelengths absorbed reflects the electron energy levels of the molecule, not heating.
questions.explain: Electron energy levels are discrete, so a photon is absorbed only if its energy matches the gap between the ground state and an available excited state. Blue and red photons match transitions in chlorophyll a; green photons do not, and are reflected or transmitted.

questions.q: Pure chlorophyll a absorbs very little light at 550 nm (green), yet the action spectrum of a whole leaf shows a rate of photosynthesis at 550 nm of about 30% of the maximum. Which explanation is best?
options: The reading must be an error, because leaves reflect green light and so cannot photosynthesize in it at all.
In a living leaf chlorophyll a absorbs green light strongly, which is the reason the leaf appears green to the eye.
Green light warms the leaf, and the higher temperature speeds up the enzyme-catalysed reactions of photosynthesis.
Accessory pigments absorb some of the green light that chlorophyll a does not, and pass the energy on.
optionWhy: A student who turns 'absorbs little green' into 'absorbs none' picks this. Leaves reflect much of the green light but absorb some, so a reduced but real rate in green light is expected, not an error.
A student who thinks a pigment absorbs the colour it shows picks this. Chlorophyll a absorbs green poorly in the leaf as in the test tube; the leaf looks green because green light is reflected.

A student who thinks light acts through heating picks this. Photosynthesis is driven by photons absorbed by pigments that excite electrons; warming does not explain a rate of photosynthesis in a specific wavelength.

This is a key difference between the two spectra: the action spectrum of a leaf reflects all its pigments. Accessory pigments absorb wavelengths that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly, including part of the green region, so photosynthesis continues at a reduced rate in green light.
questions.explain: This is a key difference between the two spectra: the action spectrum of a leaf reflects all its pigments. Accessory pigments absorb wavelengths that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly, including part of the green region, so photosynthesis continues at a reduced rate in green light.

questions.q: In an enclosed greenhouse trial, wheat grown at 550 ppm carbon dioxide gave 35% more grain than wheat at 370 ppm. In a FACE experiment with the same variety in open fields, plots at 550 ppm gave 13% more grain than plots at 370 ppm. Which is the best explanation of the difference?
options: Other factors, such as water and nitrogen supply, also limit growth in the field, so the extra carbon dioxide gives a smaller gain.
The FACE result is unreliable because weather and soil could not be held constant, so only the greenhouse figure should be used to predict future yields.
The response of a variety to carbon dioxide is a fixed property of that variety, so the FACE plots must in fact have received less than 550 ppm carbon dioxide.
Wheat grown in the field obtains most of its extra mass from soil minerals rather than from carbon dioxide, so enrichment matters less there than in a greenhouse.
optionWhy: In natural conditions growth is limited by several factors at once, so raising carbon dioxide alone has a smaller effect than under idealised greenhouse conditions. This is why field experiments such as FACE are needed to predict future plant growth realistically.

A student who thinks only a fully controlled experiment is valid picks this. FACE uses control plots at ambient carbon dioxide in the same field, so weather and soil affect both treatments equally; the field result is the more realistic guide to future yields.

A student who assumes a greenhouse response applies anywhere picks this. The same variety responds differently in the field because other limiting factors are present; the difference does not imply an error in the treatment.

A student who thinks plant mass comes from the soil picks this. The carbon in grain comes from carbon dioxide fixed in photosynthesis in the field just as in the greenhouse; soil minerals supply no carbon.
questions.explain: In natural conditions growth is limited by several factors at once, so raising carbon dioxide alone has a smaller effect than under idealised greenhouse conditions. This is why field experiments such as FACE are needed to predict future plant growth realistically.

questions.q: Photolysis of water by cyanobacteria began releasing oxygen into the oceans and atmosphere more than two billion years ago. Which statement describes a consequence of this?
options: Oxygen benefited all the organisms living at the time, because every one of them was able to switch from anaerobic to aerobic respiration.
Oxygen oxidized dissolved iron, forming banded iron formations in rocks, and was toxic to many of the anaerobic organisms living at the time.
Oxygen levels did not rise until land plants evolved, because bacteria release too little oxygen to affect the atmosphere.
The oxygen released came from carbon dioxide, so atmospheric carbon dioxide fell by exactly the amount that oxygen rose.
optionWhy: A student who assumes oxygen has always been good for life picks this. Early organisms were anaerobes with no protection against oxygen, and many were killed by it; aerobic respiration evolved later.

The advent of oxygen generation had immense consequences for geological processes and living organisms: dissolved iron in the oceans was oxidized and deposited as banded iron formations, and free oxygen was toxic to the anaerobes that dominated the early Earth, causing widespread extinction before aerobic life spread.
A student who attributes atmospheric oxygen to plants picks this. Cyanobacteria oxygenated the oceans and atmosphere more than a billion years before plants colonised the land.

A student who thinks oxygen is stripped from carbon dioxide picks this. The oxygen released by photolysis comes from water; carbon dioxide levels changed through carbon fixation, not by giving up their oxygen.
questions.explain: The advent of oxygen generation had immense consequences for geological processes and living organisms: dissolved iron in the oceans was oxidized and deposited as banded iron formations, and free oxygen was toxic to the anaerobes that dominated the early Earth, causing widespread extinction before aerobic life spread.

questions.q: What happens to reduced NADP after it has been formed by photosystem I?
options: It passes its electrons to the chain of carriers so that protons are pumped, as reduced NAD does in mitochondria.
It supplies the phosphate and energy needed to convert triose phosphate back into RuBP in the stroma.
It carries electrons and hydrogen into the stroma, where they reduce glycerate 3-phosphate to triose phosphate.
It is stored in the stroma until darkness falls, when the light-independent reactions are able to use it.
optionWhy: A student who transfers the role of reduced NAD in respiration picks this. In the chloroplast the chain reduces NADP as its last step; reduced NADP does not feed electrons back into it.
A student who has paired the two products with the two energy-requiring steps the wrong way round picks this. Regeneration of RuBP uses ATP only; reduced NADP is used to reduce glycerate 3-phosphate.

Reduced NADP is the product of the light-dependent reactions. It is used in the stroma by the light-independent reactions, where it reduces glycerate 3-phosphate to triose phosphate, and the NADP released returns to be reduced again.
A student who thinks the light-independent reactions happen at night picks this. Reduced NADP is used as soon as it forms; the Calvin cycle runs in the light and stops soon after light is removed.
questions.explain: Reduced NADP is the product of the light-dependent reactions. It is used in the stroma by the light-independent reactions, where it reduces glycerate 3-phosphate to triose phosphate, and the NADP released returns to be reduced again.

questions.q: Illuminated chloroplasts are deprived of carbon dioxide. Photosystem II soon stops emitting electrons. Which explanation is correct?
options: Only the Calvin cycle is affected; the light-dependent reactions continue at their full rate and store up ATP and reduced NADP for later use.
Carbon dioxide is the molecule split by photosystem II to obtain its electrons and oxygen, so without it there is no source of electrons.
Without carbon dioxide no ATP can be made, and ATP is what powers the emission of electrons from the reaction centre of photosystem II.
The Calvin cycle stops using ATP and reduced NADP, so NADP and ADP are not regenerated; electrons cannot leave photosystem I and the chain backs up to photosystem II.
optionWhy: A student who treats the two stages as independent picks this. The light-dependent reactions need NADP and ADP returned by the Calvin cycle; when these run out, electron flow and photosystem II stop, as observed.

A student who thinks oxygen and electrons come from carbon dioxide picks this. Photosystem II splits water, not carbon dioxide; the effect of removing carbon dioxide is indirect, through the failure to regenerate NADP.

A student who thinks ATP powers the light-dependent reactions picks this. Photosystem II is driven by light; it stops because the chain of carriers beyond it is blocked when NADP is no longer regenerated, not for lack of ATP.

The two stages are interdependent. Without carbon dioxide there is no glycerate 3-phosphate to reduce, so reduced NADP is not used and no NADP is available to accept electrons from photosystem I. Electrons accumulate along the chain, and photosystem II can no longer pass on or replace its electrons, so it stops functioning.
questions.explain: The two stages are interdependent. Without carbon dioxide there is no glycerate 3-phosphate to reduce, so reduced NADP is not used and no NADP is available to accept electrons from photosystem I. Electrons accumulate along the chain, and photosystem II can no longer pass on or replace its electrons, so it stops functioning.
